name: GO Classes Test Series 2023 | Theory of Computation | Test 4

question.text:
Consider languages $\text{L}$ and $\text{L}_{1}$, each over the alphabet $\Sigma=\{a, b\}$, where
$$
\text{L}_{1}=\left\{w \mid w \text { contains some } \mathrm{x} \in \text{L} \text { as a substring; } w \in \Sigma^{\ast}\right\}
$$
Which of the following must be true about $\text{L}$ and $\text{L}_{1}?$

  1. If $\text{L}$ is regular, then $\text{L}_{1}$ is regular.
  2. If $\text{L}$ is context-free, then $\text{L}_{1}$ is context-free.
  3. If $\text{L}$ is recursive, then $\text{L}_{1}$ is recursive.
  4. If $\text{L}$ is regular then $\text{L}_{1}$ may be non- regular.

Assume that <stmt>, <cond>, and <tail> are

nonterminal symbols, and if, then, else, true, false, skip, fi are terminal symbols.

Which of the following sets of productions determine(s) an ambiguous context-free grammar?

  1. <stmt> → if <cond> then <stmt>
<stmt> → if <cond> then <stmt> else <stmt>
<stmt> → skip
<cond> → true | false

  2. <stmt> → if <cond> then <stmt> fi
<stmt> → if <cond> then <stmt> else <stmt> fi
<stmt> → skip
<cond> → true | false
  3. <stmt> → if <cond> then <stmt> <tail>
<stmt> → skip
<cond> → true | false
<tail> → ε
<tail> → else <stmt>
  1. I only
  2. II only
  3. II and III only
  4. I and III only

Let $P(\Sigma^ \ast)$ denote the set of all languages over the alphabet $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$. We define a function $f$ from $P(\Sigma^ \ast)$ to $P(\Sigma^ \ast)$. For any language $\text{L}$ in $P(\Sigma^ \ast)$, the function $f$ replaces all $1's$ by $0 's$ (and leaves the $0 's$ as they are) in every string of $\text{L}$ to get $f(\text{L})$.

For instance, if $\text{L}=\{\epsilon, 001,00,11,111,1100\}$, then $f(\mathrm{L})=\{\epsilon, 000,00,0000\}$

Consider the following statements:

  • $\mathrm{S}1:$ If $\text{L}$ is regular then $f(\text{L})$ is regular.
  • $\mathrm{S}2:$ If $f(\mathrm{L})$ is regular then $\mathrm{L}$ is regular.

Which of the above statements is correct?

  1. Only $\mathrm{S}1$
  2. Only $\mathrm{S} 2$
  3. Both
  4. None

Consider the following languages :

  • $\mathrm{L}=\left\{w \in\{0,1\}^{\ast} \mid w\right.$ is the binary encoding of $\left.2^{k}, k>0\right\}$
  • $\mathrm{M}=\left\{w \in\{1\}^{\ast} \mid w\right.$ is the unary encoding of $\left.2^{k}, k>0\right\}$

Which of the above languages is Regular?

  1. Only $\text{L}$
  2. Only $\text{M}$
  3. Both
  4. None

Which of the following is/are true?

  1. The union of all finite subsets of a regular language is regular.
  2. The union of all infinite subsets of an infinite regular language is regular.
  3. The union of all subsets of a regular language is regular.
  4. For every infinite CFL $\text{L},$ At least one proper infinite subset of $\text{L}$ is regular.

Let $\Sigma ^\ast$ denote the set of all languages over the alphabet $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$. We define a function $f$ from $\Sigma ^\ast$ to $\Sigma ^\ast$. For any language $\text{L}$ in $\Sigma^{\ast}, f(\mathrm{L})$ is the language formed from $\text{L}$ by changing every $0$ to $1$ and every $1$ to $0$ (simultaneously) in every string of $\text{L}.$

For instance, if $\mathrm{L}=\{\epsilon, 001,00,11,01\}$, then $f(\mathrm{L})=\{\epsilon, 110,11,00,10\}$

Consider the following statements:

  • $\text{S1}:$ If $\text{L}$ is regular then $f(\text{L})$ is regular.
  • $\text{S2}:$ If $f(\mathrm{L})$ is regular then $\mathrm{L}$ is regular.

Which of the above statements is correct?

  1. Only $\text{S1}$
  2. Only $\text{S2}$
  3. Both
  4. None

Set of all Non-regular languages is/are closed under which of the following operations?

  1. Union
  2. Intersection
  3. Complementation
  4. Reversal

Consider a regular language $\text{L}$ over $\{0,1\}$. Which of the following languages over $\{0,1\}$ must also be regular?

  1. $\{w \in L \mid$ the length of $w$ is even $\}$
  2. $\{w \in L \mid$ the length of $w$ is prime $\}$
  3. $\{w \in L \mid$ the length of $w$ is an integer power of $2\}$

 

  1. I only
  2. III only
  3. I and III only
  4. I, II, and III

Consider the following statements :

  1. No infinite subset of $\left\{a^{n} b^{n} \mid \mathrm{n}>0\right\}$ is regular.
  2. No infinite subset of $\left\{w w \mid w \in\{a, b\}^{\ast}\right\}$ is regular.

Which of the above statements is/are true?

  1. Only $1$
  2. Only $2$
  3. Both
  4. None

Set of all finite languages is/are closed under which of the following operations?

  1. Union
  2. Set Difference
  3. Complementation
  4. Subset

Consider the following two languages.
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\text{L}_{1}=\left\{x \in\{a, b\}^{\ast} \mid x \text { has equally many } a \text { 's and } b \text { 's }\right\} \\
&\text{L}_{2}=\left\{x \in\{a, b, c\}^{\ast} \mid x \text { has equally many } a \text { 's, } b \text { 's, and } c \text { 's }\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$
Which of the following is true about $\text{L}_{1}$ and $\text{L}_{2}?$ 

  1. $\text{L}_{1}$ and $\text{L}_{2}$ are both regular.
  2. $\text{L}_{1}$ is regular, and $\text{L}_{2}$ is context-free but not regular.
  3. Neither $\text{L}_{1}$ nor $\text{L}_{2}$ is regular, but both are context-free.
  4. $\text{L}_{1}$ is context-free but not regular, and $\text{L}_{2}$ is not context-free.

Consider the following statements :

  1. If $\mathrm{L}=\text{L}_{1}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{L}$ is context-free, then $\text{L}_{1}$ must be context-free.
  2. A context-free grammar in Chomsky's normal form is always unambiguous.

Which of the above statements are true?

  1. Both
  2. Only $1$
  3. Only $2$
  4. None

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathrm{L}_{1}=\left\{w w^{\text{R}} \mid w \in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\right\} \\
&\mathrm{L}_{2}=\left\{w \mathrm{c} w^{\text{R}} \mid w \in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\right\} \\
&\mathrm{L}_{3}=\left\{w w \mid w \in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\right\} \\
\end{aligned}
$$
Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. $\text{L}_{1}$ is deterministic CFL
  2. $\text{L}_{2}$ is deterministic CFL
  3. $\text{L}_{3}$ is a CFL but not a deterministic CFL
  4. $\text{L}_{3}$ is deterministic CFL

Consider the following language over the alphabet $\{a,b \}$:

$\mathrm{L}=\{xy \mid$ $x,y \in \{a,b \}^* $ and there are twice as many $a's$ in $x$ as in $y\}$

Which of the following is true for $\text{L}?$

  1. $\text{L}$ is regular.
  2. $\mathrm{L}$ is not regular But $\mathrm{L}$ is DCFL.
  3. $\text{L}$ is CFL but Not DCFL.
  4. $\text{L}$ is Not CFL.

Consider the following languages :

  1. $\left\{a^{m} b^{n} \mid m, n \in \mathbb{N}\right\}$
  2. $\left\{a^{m} b^{n} \mid m \leqslant n\right\}$
  3. $\left\{a^{m} b^{n} \mid m+n \leqslant 4\right\}$

Which of the above languages is regular?

  1. Only $a$
  2. Only $c$
  3. Only $a,c$
  4. All

Consider the following context-free grammar $\mathrm{G}:$
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\text{S} \rightarrow \text{A S} \mid b \\
&\text{A} \rightarrow \text{A A}|a| b \\
&\text{B} \rightarrow \text{B B} \mid a
\end{aligned}
$$
The complement of the language generated by $\mathrm{G}$ is?

  1. Regular
  2. Context Free
  3. Context Sensitive
  4. Recursive
